eras.name: 史前與原住民族
eras.summary: Thousands of years of Austronesian settlement before written records.
paragraphs: People have lived on Taiwan for at least 20,000 years. The oldest known remains belong to the Changbin culture ([[長濱文化]]) on the east coast, a Stone Age people who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering.

About 6,000 years ago, farmers of the Dabenkeng culture ([[大坌坑文化]]) appeared. Many scholars see them as ancestors of the Austronesian peoples ([[南島語族]]), whose languages later spread from Taiwan across the Pacific and Indian Oceans, as far as Madagascar, Hawaii and New Zealand. The Beinan site ([[卑南遺址]]) near Taitung, with its slate coffins and jade ornaments, is the largest prehistoric village found in Taiwan.

When Europeans arrived in the 1600s, the island was home to many Indigenous peoples ([[原住民族]]). The plains peoples ([[平埔族]]) of the west were the first to meet traders and settlers. Today 16 Indigenous peoples are officially recognised, among them the Amis ([[阿美族]]), the largest, and the Atayal ([[泰雅族]]).

eras.name: 荷西時期
eras.summary: European trading posts in the south and north.
paragraphs: Portuguese sailors are said to have called the island Ilha Formosa, "beautiful island" ([[福爾摩沙]]). The first Europeans to settle were the Dutch East India Company ([[荷蘭東印度公司]]), which in 1624 built Fort Zeelandia ([[熱蘭遮城]]) at Tayouan ([[大員]]), today's Anping in Tainan. The name Taiwan probably comes from Tayouan.

The Dutch ruled the southwest as a trading colony, exporting deer hides and sugar and bringing in farm workers from Fujian. They built Fort Provintia, today's Chihkan Tower ([[赤崁樓]]). Missionaries wrote the Siraya language in Latin letters; contracts in this script, the Sinckan manuscripts ([[新港文書]]), were used for over a century. Chinese farmers rose against heavy taxes under Guo Huaiyi ([[郭懷一]]) in 1652; the revolt was crushed.
Spain held the north from 1626, around Keelung and Tamsui, until the Dutch drove them out in 1642.

eras.name: 明鄭時期
eras.summary: Koxinga drives out the Dutch; Ming loyalists rule from Tainan.
paragraphs: As the Ming dynasty fell to the Qing, the Ming loyalist commander Koxinga ([[鄭成功]]) crossed from Xiamen with his fleet in 1661. After a nine-month siege, the Dutch surrendered Fort Zeelandia in early 1662. Koxinga died a few months later, but he is still honoured in Taiwan as "Lord of the Imperial Surname" ([[國姓爺]]).

His son Zheng Jing ([[鄭經]]) ruled the Kingdom of Tungning ([[東寧王國]]) from Tainan. His adviser Chen Yonghua ([[陳永華]]) brought Chinese government and schooling: Tainan's Confucius Temple ([[孔廟]]), built in 1666, is known as "Taiwan's first school".
In 1683 the Qing admiral Shi Lang ([[施琅]]), a former officer of Koxinga, won the battle of Penghu, and Tungning surrendered.

eras.name: 清領時期
eras.summary: Two centuries of migration from Fujian and Guangdong, frontier revolts, and late modernisation.
paragraphs: The Qing made Taiwan a prefecture ([[臺灣府]]) of Fujian. For a long time it limited migration ([[渡臺禁令]]), but people from Fujian and Guangdong kept crossing the dangerous strait. The saying "crossing from Tangshan to Taiwan" ([[唐山過臺灣]]) remembers them. Many were single young men without land or family, called luohanjiao ([[羅漢腳]]).

The frontier was hard to govern: "a small revolt every three years, a big one every five". The largest, led by Lin Shuangwen ([[林爽文]]) in 1786, took more than a year to put down. Settlers from different places, such as Zhangzhou, Quanzhou and Hakka villages, also fought each other in armed feuds ([[械鬥]]).

After 1860 Taiwan's ports were opened to foreign trade ([[開港通商]]), and tea, sugar and camphor ([[樟腦]]) became major exports. The Canadian missionary George Leslie Mackay ([[馬偕]]) founded churches, schools and a hospital in Tamsui. After Japan invaded the south in the Mudan incident ([[牡丹社事件]]) of 1874, the Qing took Taiwan more seriously: Shen Baozhen ([[沈葆楨]]) strengthened its defences, and in 1885 Taiwan became a province ([[臺灣省]]). Its first governor, Liu Mingchuan ([[劉銘傳]]), built Taiwan's first railway and telegraph lines.

eras.name: 日治時期
eras.summary: Fifty years as Japan's first colony: resistance, modernisation and assimilation.
paragraphs: After losing the First Sino-Japanese War, the Qing gave Taiwan to Japan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki ([[馬關條約]]) of 1895. Local leaders declared the short-lived Republic of Formosa ([[臺灣民主國]]), and armed resistance went on for years.

Japan ruled through a Governor-General ([[總督府]]), whose office building in Taipei is today's Presidential Office. Under officials like Gotō Shinpei ([[後藤新平]]), Taiwan got a census, land surveys, public health measures, and the north–south railway. The engineer Hatta Yoichi ([[八田與一]]) built the Chianan irrigation system ([[嘉南大圳]]), which turned the southern plain into farmland.

Indigenous resistance continued in the mountains. In the Musha (Wushe) incident ([[霧社事件]]) of 1930, Seediq warriors led by Mona Rudao ([[莫那魯道]]) attacked a Japanese school sports day; the army's revenge killed hundreds. In the 1920s, Taiwanese intellectuals such as Chiang Wei-shui ([[蔣渭水]]) and Lin Hsien-tang ([[林獻堂]]) campaigned peacefully for self-rule through the Taiwanese Cultural Association ([[臺灣文化協會]]). From 1937, during the war with China, the Kōminka movement ([[皇民化運動]]) pushed Japanese language, names and religion.

eras.name: 戰後與二二八
eras.english: The end of the war and the 228 Incident
eras.summary: The Republic of China takes over; 228 and the move of the ROC government to Taiwan.
paragraphs: After Japan's surrender, the Republic of China ([[中華民國]]), led by the Nationalist Party, the KMT ([[國民黨]]), took over Taiwan in October 1945. The ROC calls this the Retrocession ([[臺灣光復]]). Many Taiwanese welcomed it at first, but the new administration under Chen Yi ([[陳儀]]) was soon resented for corruption, inflation and discrimination against locals.

On 27 February 1947, agents in Taipei beat a woman selling untaxed cigarettes and shot a bystander. Protests spread across the island the next day. The government sent troops from China, and thousands of people, including many of Taiwan's educated elite, were killed or disappeared. The 228 Incident ([[二二八事件]]) was not discussed openly for forty years; 28 February is now Peace Memorial Day.

Meanwhile the KMT was losing the Chinese Civil War ([[國共內戰]]) to the Communists. In 1949 the ROC government moved to Taipei, together with one to two million soldiers and civilians. That October, the defeat of a Communist landing on Kinmen at Guningtou ([[古寧頭戰役]]) helped keep Kinmen and Taiwan under the ROC.

eras.name: 戒嚴與白色恐怖
eras.english: Martial law and the White Terror
eras.summary: Thirty-eight years of martial law; diplomatic isolation; the rise of the opposition.
paragraphs: From 1949 to 1987 Taiwan was under martial law ([[戒嚴]]), one of the longest periods in modern history. Chiang Kai-shek ([[蔣介石]]) ruled as president until his death in 1975, and the ROC still claimed to be the government of all China. In the White Terror ([[白色恐怖]]), tens of thousands of people were imprisoned for suspected communism or support for Taiwanese independence, many on Green Island ([[綠島]]). The editor Lei Chen ([[雷震]]) was jailed in 1960 for trying to start an opposition party.

Taiwan stayed on the front line of the Cold War. In 1958 China shelled Kinmen for weeks in the 823 Artillery Battle ([[八二三砲戰]]). Families who came with the army often lived in military villages ([[眷村]]); the difference between "mainlanders" ([[外省人]]) and those already in Taiwan ([[本省人]]) shaped politics for decades.

In 1971 the ROC left the United Nations ([[退出聯合國]]) as the seat of China passed to the People's Republic, and in 1979 the United States cut official ties ([[中美斷交]]). The US Congress then passed the Taiwan Relations Act ([[臺灣關係法]]). Later that year, a human rights rally organised by the opposition magazine Formosa in Kaohsiung ended in arrests: the Formosa Incident ([[美麗島事件]]). Its defendants and their lawyers became leaders of the opposition ([[黨外]]).

eras.name: 經濟奇蹟
eras.summary: Land reform, export factories and the chip industry.
paragraphs: Land reform in the early 1950s, including rent reduction ([[三七五減租]]) and "land to the tiller" ([[耕者有其田]]), turned tenants into owners and freed capital for industry. With US aid ([[美援]]), Taiwan moved from farming to light industry.

In 1966 Kaohsiung opened one of the world's first export processing zones ([[加工出口區]]), and "Made in Taiwan" toys, textiles and electronics spread around the world. In the 1970s Premier Chiang Ching-kuo ([[蔣經國]]) launched the Ten Major Construction Projects ([[十大建設]]): the first freeway, a new airport, ports, steel mills and shipyards.

The government then backed high technology. Hsinchu Science Park ([[新竹科學園區]]) opened in 1980, and in 1987 Morris Chang ([[張忠謀]]) founded TSMC ([[台積電]]), now the world's largest chip maker. With South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore, Taiwan was one of the Four Asian Tigers ([[亞洲四小龍]]).

eras.name: 民主化
eras.summary: From one-party rule to the first direct presidential election.
paragraphs: In 1986 opposition activists founded the Democratic Progressive Party ([[民主進步黨]]) while parties were still banned; the government tolerated it. The next year Chiang Ching-kuo lifted martial law ([[解嚴]]), and in 1988 the ban on new newspapers ([[報禁]]) ended. In 1989 the publisher Nylon Deng ([[鄭南榕]]) set himself on fire rather than be arrested; his death day, 7 April, is now Freedom of Speech Day.

Lee Teng-hui ([[李登輝]]), the first Taiwan-born president, took over in 1988. In March 1990, thousands of students occupied the square in front of the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall in the Wild Lily student movement ([[野百合學運]]). Lee met their demands: the members of parliament elected in China in 1947, who had never faced re-election, retired, and the whole legislature was elected in Taiwan in 1991–1992. National Health Insurance ([[全民健保]]) started in 1995.

In 1996 Taiwan held its first direct presidential election ([[總統直選]]). China fired missiles into the sea near Taiwan in the months before ([[臺海飛彈危機]]), and the US sent aircraft carriers. Lee won with 54% of the vote.

eras.name: 當代臺灣
eras.summary: Peaceful changes of power, protests and new rights.
paragraphs: On 21 September 1999, the Chi-Chi earthquake ([[九二一大地震]]) killed about 2,400 people in central Taiwan and led to stricter building rules.

In 2000 Chen Shui-bian ([[陳水扁]]) of the DPP won the presidency, ending more than fifty years of KMT rule: the first peaceful transfer of power between parties ([[政黨輪替]]). Ma Ying-jeou ([[馬英九]]) of the KMT won in 2008 and brought closer economic ties with China. In 2014 students occupied the Legislative Yuan for over three weeks to stop a services trade agreement with China: the Sunflower Movement ([[太陽花學運]]).

Tsai Ing-wen ([[蔡英文]]) became Taiwan's first woman president in 2016. In 2019 Taiwan became the first place in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage ([[同性婚姻]]). Lai Ching-te ([[賴清德]]) of the DPP followed as president in 2024.
